notes.meaning: The high priest asked Stephen if the accusations brought against him were true. Stephen was on trial before the Jewish high council, charged with speaking against the temple and the law of Moses. Instead of simply pleading guilty or not guilty, Stephen used this moment to give a clear testimony about God's plan.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The charges against Stephen were twisted versions of things he had actually taught, such as Jesus foretelling the temple's destruction and God not living in temples made by hands.

notes.meaning: Stephen spoke with great respect, calling the council members his brothers and fathers. He reminded them that the glorious God appeared to Abraham far away in Mesopotamia, long before Abraham ever set foot in the Promised Land. This showed right away that God's presence was never limited to the temple or to a single country. Abraham was told to leave his home and follow God in simple faith.

Abraham obeyed God's call and moved first from Ur to Haran. After his father died, God led him into the land of Canaan, where the council was now living. True faith meant trusting God one step at a time, moving wherever God directed.

God did not give Abraham any land to own at that time, not even a single foot of ground. Yet God promised that the entire land would belong to him and his future children, even though Abraham did not have any children yet. Abraham had to live as a traveler and trust God's bare promise completely.

God warned Abraham that his family would live in a foreign land as mistreated slaves for four hundred years. But God also promised to punish the nation that enslaved them and bring His people out to worship Him. God's people can trust that He sees their suffering and will always keep His word to rescue them.

God gave Abraham circumcision as a visible sign of their covenant, which was God's sacred agreement with him. Abraham then circumcised his son Isaac, who became the father of Jacob, who in turn fathered the twelve leaders of the tribes of Israel. Stephen showed that God's covenant began by grace long before the temple was ever built.

The twelve brothers grew jealous of Joseph and sold him into slavery in Egypt, but God remained with Joseph through it all. God rescued him from prison and gave him great wisdom, leading Pharaoh to put him in charge of the whole kingdom. Joseph's story is the first example Stephen gives of Israel rejecting God's chosen leader, whom God later exalted.

A terrible famine struck both Egypt and Canaan, leaving Jacob's family without food. When Jacob heard that grain was stored in Egypt, he sent his sons there to buy food, but they did not recognize Joseph on their first trip. On their second trip, Joseph revealed who he was, and his family was introduced to Pharaoh. Just as the brothers had to return to the brother they had rejected, Israel would need to turn to the Savior they had turned away.

Joseph sent for his father Jacob and his whole family, counting seventy-five people in all. Stephen used the number found in the Greek translation of the Old Testament, which counted several more of Joseph's descendants. God took care of this small family and grew them into a great nation.

Jacob went down to Egypt, where he and all his sons eventually died. Their remains were later taken back to Canaan and buried in the tomb Abraham had bought from Hamor's family at Shechem. Even in death, the patriarchs showed their faith that God would one day give the land to their people.

As the time for God to fulfill His promise approached, the Israelites grew rapidly in number in Egypt. Then a new king took power who had no loyalty to Joseph's memory and treated the people with cruel cunning. He forced the parents to abandon their baby boys outdoors so they would die.

Moses was born during this dark time of persecution, and God saw that he was a very special child. His parents hid and cared for him at home for three months. When they could hide him no longer and had to put him outside, Pharaoh's daughter found him and raised him as her own son.

Growing up in Pharaoh's palace, Moses received the highest education Egypt could offer. He became powerful both in what he said and in what he accomplished. God used this royal training to prepare Moses for the great leadership tasks ahead.

When Moses was forty years old, he chose to visit his own people and check on their suffering. Seeing an Egyptian beating a Hebrew slave, Moses defended his countryman and struck the oppressor down. Moses assumed his people would understand that God was using him to deliver them, but they did not grasp it yet.

The very next day, Moses tried to stop two Israelites who were fighting each other, reminding them that they were brothers. But the man in the wrong shoved Moses away and asked who made him ruler and judge over them. He then asked if Moses planned to kill him just like he had killed the Egyptian the day before.

When Moses realized his deed was known, he fled from Egypt to escape Pharaoh's anger. He settled as a foreigner in the desert land of Midian, where he married and had two sons. God kept Moses safe during those quiet desert years while getting him ready for his real life's work.

After forty years had passed in the desert, an angel appeared to Moses in the flames of a bush near Mount Sinai. The bush burned brightly without burning up, showing God's holy presence out in the barren wilderness. God revealed Himself far from Jerusalem and the temple, proving once more that His holy presence is not tied to any building.

differ.view: The angel of the Lord in the burning bush was the Son of God Himself appearing before He came in human flesh.
